chmmc-2017-power-1-1.title: Multiply choices
chmmc-2017-power-1-1.body:
Each of the $4$ pegs can be any of $6$ colors independently: $6^4=1296$.

**Answer: 1296**

chmmc-2017-power-1-2.title: Count by $c$
chmmc-2017-power-1-2.body:
If $c=0$: $m=0,\dots,4$ gives $5$ feedbacks. If $c=1$: $m=0,\dots,3$ gives $4$. If $c=2$: $m=0,1,2$ gives $3$. If $c\ge3$: only $(3,0)$ and $(4,0)$ ($(3,1)$ is impossible, see the next part), $2$ feedbacks. Total $5+4+3+2=14$. (A computer check over all pairs of codes finds exactly these $14$ feedbacks.)

**Answer: 14**

chmmc-2017-power-1-3.title: Why $(3,1)$ fails
chmmc-2017-power-1-3.body:
Suppose $3$ pegs are in the right place. The only remaining peg of the guess is in the position where the secret has its fourth peg, so if it has the right color it is correct (giving $(4,0)$), and otherwise its color is not the one of the remaining secret peg, so it is neither correct nor misplaced (giving $(3,0)$). Hence $(3,1)$ never occurs.

**Answer: $(3,1)$**

chmmc-2017-power-2-1.title: No green
chmmc-2017-power-2-1.body:
The feedback says the secret has no G. Each of the $4$ pegs has $5$ remaining colors: $5^4=625$.

**Answer: 625**

chmmc-2017-power-2-2.title: Which peg is the correct one
chmmc-2017-power-2-2.body:
*Case 1: one of the three G's is the correct peg* ($3$ choices of which). With $0$ misplaced, the other three pegs cannot be G or Y: $4$ colors each, $4^3=64$. Total $3\cdot64=192$.

*Case 2: the Y is correct.* The first three pegs cannot be G (no G at all, else a G would be correct or misplaced): $5^3=125$.

Total $192+125=317$. (Confirmed by brute-force counting over all $1296$ codes.)

**Answer: 317**

chmmc-2017-power-2-3.title: Choose the correct peg
chmmc-2017-power-2-3.body:
There are $4$ choices for which guess peg is the single correct one. Since nothing is misplaced, the other three secret pegs cannot be G or Y: $4$ colors each. Total $4\cdot4^3=256$.

**Answer: 256**

chmmc-2017-power-2-4a.title: Read off the composition
chmmc-2017-power-2-4a.body:
The secret has no R, G, Y; exactly two B's and one O. The remaining peg must then be V. So the code is an arrangement of B, B, O, V, and every arrangement is consistent. Count $\frac{4!}{2!\,1!\,1!}=12$.

**Answer: 12**

chmmc-2017-power-2-4b.title: Composition then positions
chmmc-2017-power-2-4b.body:
The first four guesses show exactly one each of R, B, Y, G. The last three show the secret has no O (the O's give no feedback) and that R, B, G are not in position $1$ (otherwise that first peg would be correct, not misplaced). So position $1$ is Y, and the other three pegs are a permutation of R, B, G. Count $3!=6$.

**Answer: 6**

chmmc-2017-power-2-4c.title: Exactly two R and two B
chmmc-2017-power-2-4c.body:
The first feedback accounts for all four pegs of the guess, so the secret contains exactly two R's and two B's, and since all colors are matched, $m=4-c$; we need $c=2$ for both guesses. There are only six arrangements of $RRBB$. Comparing positionwise with the guesses RRBB and RBBR: RRBB gives $(4,0)$ and $(2,2)$; RBRB gives $c=2$ and $c=2$; RBBR gives $c=2$ and $c=4$; BRRB gives $c=2$ and $c=0$; BRBR gives $c=2$ and $c=2$; BBRR gives $c=0$ and $c=2$. Only RBRB and BRBR work, so $2$ codes remain.

**Answer: 2**

chmmc-2017-power-3-1.title: One color at a time
chmmc-2017-power-3-1.body: Guess the six monochrome codes RRRR, OOOO, YYYY, GGGG, BBBB, VVVV in this order. For a guess CCCC, the secret's number of C pegs is exactly the number of correct pegs (and the misplaced count is always $0$). After at most $6$ guesses the composition is known.

chmmc-2017-power-3-2.title: Skip the last color
chmmc-2017-power-3-2.body: Guess RRRR, OOOO, YYYY, GGGG, BBBB, in this order. Each tells how many pegs of its color the secret has. The remaining $4-(\text{total found})$ pegs must be V. So $5$ guesses suffice.

chmmc-2017-power-3-3.title: Test two colors at once
chmmc-2017-power-3-3.body: Guess RRBB. If any peg is correct, the secret is RRRR or BBBB: guess RRRR, then BBBB (at most $3$ guesses in all). Otherwise guess OOGG. If any peg is correct, the secret is OOOO or GGGG: guess these in turn (at most $4$ guesses). Otherwise the secret is YYYY or VVVV, guess them in turn (at most $4$ guesses). So at most $4\le5$ guesses are needed.

chmmc-2017-power-3-4.title: Use three colors in one guess
chmmc-2017-power-3-4.body: Guess RROY. Feedback $(2,0)$: the secret is RRRR (it would have $2$ correct pegs), so guess RRRR (guess $2$). Feedback $(1,0)$: the secret is OOOO or YYYY; guess both (at most guess $3$). Feedback $(0,0)$: the secret is GGGG, BBBB or VVVV. Guess GGGB: feedback $(3,0)$ means GGGG (guess $3$), $(1,0)$ means BBBB (guess $3$), and $(0,0)$ means VVVV (guess $3$). In every case at most $3$ guesses are used.

chmmc-2017-power-3-5.title: Guess everything
chmmc-2017-power-3-5.body: There are $6^4=1296<1300$ codes. Guess them one by one in any fixed order; the secret is reached within $1296$ guesses.

chmmc-2017-power-3-6.title: Composition, then arrangements
chmmc-2017-power-3-6.body: Use the six guesses RRRR, ..., VVVV to find the color composition (problem 3.1). Now the secret is an arrangement of a known multiset of $4$ pegs, so there are at most $4!=24$ possibilities. Guess them one by one. Total at most $6+24=30$ guesses.

chmmc-2017-power-3-7.title: Narrow the first peg
chmmc-2017-power-3-7.body: Find the composition in $6$ guesses. Pick a color $X$ not in the secret (some color is missing, since there are $6$ colors and only $4$ pegs). Let $C,D,\dots$ be the colors in the secret. Guess $CXXX$ and $DXXX$ (if there is only one color or two colors the problem is easier). The feedback of $CXXX$ is $(1,0)$ if the first peg is $C$ and $(0,1)$ otherwise (C is in the code); similarly for $DXXX$. So after these $2$ guesses we know whether the first peg is $C$, $D$, or neither; in the worst case the first peg is one of at most $2$ colors, and the other three pegs can be arranged in at most $3!=6$ ways. This leaves at most $2\cdot3!=12$ candidate codes. Guessing them one by one uses at most $6+2+12=20$ guesses.

chmmc-2017-power-3-8.title: Position by position
chmmc-2017-power-3-8.body: Find the color composition in $5$ guesses (problem 3.2). Some color $X$ does not occur in the secret. For position $p$, and each candidate color $c$ still available, a guess with $c$ in position $p$ and $X$ elsewhere has feedback $(1,0)$ if the secret has $c$ in position $p$, and $(0,1)$ or $(0,0)$ otherwise. In the worst case (four distinct colors $C,D,E,F$): guess $CXXX$, $DXXX$, $EXXX$ ($\le3$ guesses; if all fail the first peg is $F$) to find the first peg, say $C$; then $XDXX$, $XEXX$ ($\le2$ guesses) to find the second peg; then $XXFX$ ($1$ guess) for the third peg; the fourth is forced; then $1$ final guess for the secret. Total $5+3+2+1+1=12$. When colors repeat there are fewer candidate colors at each step, and the total is still at most $12$ (checked by running the strategy on all $1296$ codes: the worst case is exactly $12$ guesses).

chmmc-2017-power-4-1.title: Pigeonhole
chmmc-2017-power-4-1.body: After the first guess, the $1296$ possible codes are partitioned by the feedback they would produce into at most $14$ classes. Some class has at least $\lceil1296/14\rceil=93\ge80$ codes. If the actual feedback is the one for that class, at least $93$ codes remain possible. ∎

chmmc-2017-power-4-2.title: A second guess cannot be certain
chmmc-2017-power-4-2.body: For any first guess, some feedback leaves at least $80>1$ codes. If the secret is among them (and the setter gives that feedback), the second guess is a single code and is wrong for at least $79$ of them. So no strategy can guarantee a win in $2$ guesses. ∎

chmmc-2017-power-4-3.title: Pigeonhole twice
chmmc-2017-power-4-3.body: After the first guess some feedback leaves a set $S_1$ of at least $93\ge80$ codes. The second guess (made knowing the feedback) splits $S_1$ into at most $14$ classes by feedback, so some class $S_2$ has at least $\lceil80/14\rceil=6>1$ codes (in fact at least $7$). If the secret lies in $S_2$ and these feedbacks are produced, then at the third guess there are at least $6$ codes still possible, so the single third guess cannot be guaranteed to be correct. Hence no strategy wins within $3$ guesses. ∎
